items.title: Saving Private Jensen!
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: Happy Thanksgiving, everyone! And here’s our latest update on how the Silicon Valley right insists that Jensen Huang has been framed.

items.title: Inside the Silicon Valley vs. DC Myth War Driving the Jensen Restoration
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: As I write this morning, the day before Thanksgiving, Nvidia stock is trading at $141 per share. That means it’s given up roughly 3/4 of the value it gained after Monday’s shock announcement that Donald Trump had, paradoxically, midwifed Jensen Huang back into the CEO suite at Nvidia. I jokingly compared Huang’s return to Napoleon’s “100 Days” between his escape from exile on Elba to his final exile at St. Helena. Maybe I was being optimistic. Today I want to pull back to a broader view of this unfolding drama, which is the collision between the cultures of Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C., the swashbuckling world of Silicon Valley and national security state.

items.title: Day Two Isn’t Looking Great for Trump or NVIDIA
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: As I write this morning, NVIDIA stock has given up roughly half of yesterday’s Jensen Restoration surge — 40 points up and 19 points down, if you’re keeping score at home. Obviously, today’s single-day fall is no more definitive than yesterday’s surge. At a minimum, though, it reflects second-day realizations that there were reasons Jensen Huang was booted in the first place: the multiple investigations noted here yesterday and all the unknowns that go with them. It will take some time to see how this gambit shakes out in terms of NVIDIA’s stock price. But everything we’ve seen so far points in the direction of an extraordinary, brute-force use of presidential power to engineer a result with decidedly short-term and evanescent gains.

items.title: Napoleon Returned to Power Too … But Not for Long
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: Okay, not doing one of these every day now. But this Jensen Huang thing just demanded a quick explainer. Can Donald Trump still command the tides? Can he command the Jensen Huang spy scandal to end? Probably not! Trump and the INVIDIA board have made themselves hostages to fortune on the assumption that Trump is still all powerful even as his power is clearly ebbing. Napoleon returned to power after he escaped from Elba too. But not for long.

items.title: Jensen Restoration Movement Scores Big Win
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content:
If you haven’t heard yet, the NVIDIA board just announced this morning that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the company. This comes 11 days after his ouster and after almost as many days in which the board and its interim CEO said there was no consideration of restoring him to power. Critically, in its press release, the board said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Needless to say this certainly means Donald J. Trump.

items.title: It’s Golden Dukes Time of Year – Golden Stefaniks?
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: If you’re a long time TPM Reader you’ll know we have a special place in our hearts for members of Congress who have mystery buyers buy their houses for wildly more than their worth. So we put together this quick explainer about the breaking story about Rep. Elise Stefanik’s mystery home buyer.

items.title: The Dictator Thing
items.author: Josh Marshall
items.content: Donald Trump’s giddiness around dictators is one of the abiding themes of his two presidencies. You can see it now in the eagerness with which he’s anticipated his summit/meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Indeed, in the last two days Trump’s been casting about for the possibility of adding Kim Jong Un to the trio. These are quite simply the men he admires the most because they embody his actual vision of what a leader should be. It’s easy to get the sense in these meetings that Vladimir Putin heads one of the world’s three great powers. But that simply isn’t the case. Russia is a comparatively minor economy. It has a lot of oil and gas. It has nuclear weapons, really the only thing that makes it a major player on the world stage. As a conventional military power it’s struggled for years to subdue even Ukraine. The U.S. and China are great powers, with mammoth economies vast enough to sustain huge militaries. Russia is really only in this group because it has become what amounts to a junior associate of China and because of Donald Trump’s fixation on it as a kind of model power. In a way, Trump’s eagerness to add Kim Jong Un to the group underlines why Russia is there in the first place.
